title: Elemental and isotopic links to Pacific oyster (Magallana gigas) growth and culture performance among farming leases
content:
Abstract

Environmental interactions fundamentally shape oyster aquaculture performance, yet the mechanistic drivers of growth variability among farming leases remain an ecological puzzle. Elemental and isotopic signatures provide fine-scale, biogeochemical proxies of environmental sourcing and trophic linkages that can help resolve this variability and inform practical site selection, management, and husbandry decisions. Here, high-resolution Itrax core scanning combined with δ13C and δ15N stable-isotope analysis of sedimentary [sediment organic matter (SOM)] and dietary [particulate organic matter (POM)] sources, and oyster flesh and shell, revealed coherent biogeochemical linkages underlying differential productivity between two prominent Pacific oyster farming estuaries in Tasmania. Fifteen elements showed clear ecological partitioning: Fe, Ca, and Sr dominated SOM; Zn and Ba characterized POM; Zn, Ca, and Fe were most enriched in oyster tissues; and Ca and Sr strongly defined shell mineralization. δ13C enrichment tracked the higher-productivity estuary, Little Swanport, across both estuary and culture period. Oysters assimilated key elements through trophic and atrophic pathways, with Zn, Ca, Fe, and Sr emerging as candidate discriminators of estuary-specific performance. Shell formation was most strongly influenced by SOM and fine-fraction POM (0.7 μm), more efficiently utilized in Little Swanport and linked accelerated tissue and shell accretion relative to Pitt Water. These findings suggest that strategic management of estuarine elemental and nutrient regimes could sustain high yields, and offer preliminary biogeochemical signatures for oyster farm site selection, optimization, and provenance determination, pending validation across a broader range of farming sites.
